## Observations

1. A final common height \(H\) costs exactly \(\sum_i(U_i+D_i)-NH\), so minimizing the cost means maximizing the feasible height.
2. The smoothness rule implies that the final upper length at position \(i\) is at most \(U_j+X|i-j|\) for every position \(j\). The minimum of these bounds, \(M_i\), is itself a valid smooth sequence of upper lengths.
3. A nonnegative integer height \(H\) is feasible exactly when \(H\le M_i+D_i\) at every position. At such a height, the final upper lengths can be chosen as \(\min(M_i,H)\).
4. Each bound \(U_j+X|i-j|\) increases by \(X\) per position away from \(j\), so all values \(M_i\) can be computed with one sweep in each direction.

## Solution sketch

> Each bound \(U_j+X|i-j|\) increases by \(X\) per position away from \(j\), so all values \(M_i\) can be computed with one sweep in each direction.

1. Copy the original upper lengths into an array \(M\). Sweep from left to right, starting at the second position, and replace each entry with the smaller of its current value and the updated entry to its left plus \(X\). This incorporates every bound from the current position and its left. Then sweep from right to left, starting at the second-to-last position, taking the smaller of the current entry and the updated entry to its right plus \(X\). This adds the bounds from the right. Any bound from the left propagated back through the right neighbor has traveled farther and cannot improve the value already found.

> The smoothness rule implies that the final upper length at position \(i\) is at most \(U_j+X|i-j|\) for every position \(j\). The minimum of these bounds, \(M_i\), is itself a valid smooth sequence of upper lengths.

2. Use the resulting \(M\) as the pointwise greatest possible smooth sequence of upper lengths. The bound follows by applying the adjacent-difference rule along the path from \(j\) to \(i\). Each bound changes by at most \(X\) between adjacent positions, so their pointwise minimum does too. Also, \(0\le M_i\le U_i\), since the bound with \(j=i\) is \(U_i\).

> A nonnegative integer height \(H\) is feasible exactly when \(H\le M_i+D_i\) at every position. At such a height, the final upper lengths can be chosen as \(\min(M_i,H)\).

3. Set \(H\) to \(\min_i(M_i+D_i)\). Each pair's final total is bounded above by \(M_i+D_i\). To see that the chosen height is attainable, cap every \(M_i\) at \(H\), which preserves smoothness, and assign the lower tooth the remaining length \(\max(0,H-M_i)\). That length is between zero and \(D_i\). This argument also covers \(H=0\) and allows individual teeth to be ground down to zero.

> A final common height \(H\) costs exactly \(\sum_i(U_i+D_i)-NH\), so minimizing the cost means maximizing the feasible height.

4. Subtract \(NH\) from the original total and print the result. Each unit of removed length costs one yen. If the teeth already fit, their original height is feasible and the formula gives zero. Use integer arithmetic that can hold totals beyond 32 bits. The sweeps and scans take \(O(N)\) time and \(O(N)\) space.
system_prompt:
You are a programming problem planner. Produce a natural-language guide
with exactly these headings:
## Observations
Give numbered, useful observations derived from the problem specification.
## Solution sketch
Describe one coherent algorithm as numbered steps. Before each step quote the
relevant observation exactly, then explain how that observation supports the step.
Cover edge cases and time/space complexity in the sketch.
Return prose only, without Python implementation or command blocks.
The guide will be implemented by a separate coding agent.

generation.note: Harness wall time includes Codex startup; not API latency.

usage.note: Codex token counts include its harness context; not comparable to API usage.

isolation.mechanism: codex exec, fresh ephemeral session, empty temporary working directory, user config and exec rules ignored, read-only sandbox, web search and listed features disabled, credential-like variables removed from the environment
isolation.limits: Codex harness instructions and its own tool descriptions remain in the model context; they cannot be removed. Tool isolation is verified post hoc from the event stream, which contained no tool, command, file or search events.
